newsitem.title: UK: Elvis industry faces UK High Court decision.
newsitem.headline: Elvis industry faces UK High Court decision.

text.p: The legend of Elvis Presley was at the centre of a legal wrangle on Monday when a British judge weighed up the right of rival business interests to promote the king of rock 'n' roll's memorabilia.
Elvis might have been turning in his grave when a bewigged judge in a dusty London courtroom examined a bar of perfumed soap and cologne bearing his portrait and signature.

British entrepreneur Sid Shaw, owner of the east London shop Elvisly Yours, which sells souvenirs of the singer, is challenging the might of Elvis Presley Enterprises of Memphis, Tennessee, who have trademarks to market Presley toiletries.
"You can't own Elvis when he belongs to the world," Shaw told Reuters after the the first day of the hearing.
Shaw says the Elvis estate wants to monopolise the Presley paraphernalia market in Britain.
He was objecting to the British Trade Marks Registry granting the Tennessee business trademarks to sell toiletries under the brands Elvis, Elvis Presley and Elvis A Presley.
"How can you monopolise the Elvis industry?" he asked. "We're talking about a massive multi-million dollar industry, how can you monopolise that? It's against the law in America."

Shaw has earnt a living since soon after the singer's death in 1977, selling Elvis soap, statues and underpants from a range of 2,000 items. Legal wranglings have grown more bitter since they began in 1985.

Shaw said his business has given the Elvis estate beneficial publicity. He referred to his "Presleynost" venture in 1989 in the former Soviet Union -- in which he took Russian women to Elvis's home, Graceland -- as an example of such publicity.

Shaw says the Elvis estate has already hampered the work of fan clubs and even Elvis impersonators who in the U.S. have to ask Elvis Presley Enterprises for permission before they can dress up in the legend's name.
This is despite a partial victory at Britain's Trade Marks Registry last year, which ruled Shaw could continue trading as Elvisly Yours from his cramped shop in Shoreditch.
Shaw said he expected the case to be concluded on Tuesday after the jury had heard all the evidence.
"I'm quietly confident," he said, adding: "Elvis is listening in."
